**OVERVIEW**  
This project classifies seven diagnostic groups from resting-state EEG features: six psychiatric disorder groups plus healthy controls.  
   
 \- Addictive Disorder  
 \- Anxiety Disorder  
 \- Mood Disorder  
 \- Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)  
 \- Schizophrenia  
 \- Trauma and Stress-Related Disorder  
 \- Healthy Controls  
   
It combines power spectral density and coherence (i.e., functional connectivity) features with three lightweight classifiers (i.e., Extreme Learning Machine, Naive Bayes, and linear Support Vector Machine) in an one-vs-all setup. The goal is to create a reproducible and interpretable alternative to black-box deep learning.  
   
   
**WHY IT MATTERS**

* **Objectivity:** Psychiatric diagnosis still depends largely on subjective clinical assessment. Objective, measurable biomarkers are needed.  
* **Multiclass:** Most EEG machine learning studies are binary (one disorder vs. healthy).   
* **Interpretability:** Deep learning models often reach high accuracy but are hard to interpret and rarely validated outside their own dataset.   
  


**DATASET**  
Secondary analysis of the public feature-level dataset from Park et al. (2021):  
   
 \- 945 participants (850 patients, 95 healthy controls)  
 \- Single centre: Seoul Metropolitan Government \- Seoul National University  
   Boramae Medical Center, Korea  
 \- 5-minute eyes-closed resting-state EEG, 19 channels (10-20 system)  
 \-1,140 EEG features per participant (power \+ coherence across six bands)

 **Class sizes:** Addictive (186), Anxiety (107), Mood (266), OCD (46), Schizophrenia (117), Trauma/Stress-Related (128), Healthy Controls (95).

**METHODS AT A GLANCE**

Features  
 \- Absolute power (prefix AB, 19 channels) and pairwise coherence (prefix COH, 171 pairs) per band.  
 \- Restricted a priori to theta, alpha, beta and high-beta bands (760, candidate features). Delta and gamma were excluded because of sensitivity to drift/ocular and muscle artefacts in pre-processed data.  
 \- Top 300 features kept by variance ranking, then z-score normalised.  
   
Models (one-vs-all)  
 \- Extreme Learning Machine (sigmoid hidden layer, pseudoinverse output weights)  
 \- Gaussian Naive Bayes (probabilistic baseline)  
 \- Linear SVM (feature importance read from model weights)  
   
Evaluation  
 \- Stratified 80/20 train/holdout split  
 \- 5-fold stratified cross-validation inside the training set  
 \- Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals  
 \- PCA and t-SNE for visualising class separability  
 \- Single-band experiments (alpha, beta, theta)  
   
Software: MATLAB R2024b (Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox, custom ELM module)

![][image1]  
![][image2] 

*  ELM had the highest testing accuracy in every class.  
*  SVM had the better precision-recall balance in most classes, with top F1 for OCD (94.00%), Anxiety (84.08%) and Schizophrenia (79.84%).  
*  Naive Bayes was consistently the weakest.  
*  Mood Disorder was the hardest class (best F1 only 66.03%). PCA and t-SNE  plots show substantial overlap between classes.  
* Theta-band features alone gave the highest single-band accuracy (91.57%), ahead of alpha (84.87%) and beta (81.60%).  
* The top SVM-weighted features were mainly coherence features (beta/high-beta and theta, e.g. frontal-temporal and occipital pairs) plus alpha power.
